title: Quadratic-form inequalities and singular values
subtitle: G2 lecture 061000 · baseline companion · needs expansion
adaptation: First-pass source-derived outline. Section excerpts and any vector equation come from the spoken lecture and its display-only mathematics appendix. Expand with worked mathematics, proofs and topic-specific diagrams.

slides.title: The problem and its setting
slides.lead: There are two common ways to compare operators.
body: A quadratic-form inequality controls the value of an operator on every input vector. A singular-value inequality controls its ordered stretching strengths. How can we pass from the first kind of statement to the second? These languages are connected, but they are not interchangeable without assumptions. Today's goal is to derive the safe implications and identify the tempting steps that fail. Our main route will be through the Gram operator. Its quadratic form is exactly the squared output length of the original map.

slides.title: Recall the positive-operator order
slides.lead: A self-adjoint operator H is positive semidefinite when its quadratic form is nonnegative on every vector.
body: That means the inner product of H x with x is at least zero for every x. For two self-adjoint operators H and K, we write H less than or equal to K in the Loewner order when K minus H is positive semidefinite. Equivalently, H's quadratic form is at most K's quadratic form on every vector. In the finite-dimensional self-adjoint setting, the min–max principle says that the ordered eigenvalues of H are at most the corresponding ordered eigenvalues of K whenever H is below K in this form order. Why? Choose any fixed trial subspace.

slides.title: Positive operators give singular-value comparisons
slides.lead: Now suppose H and K are not just self-adjoint but both positive, with H less than or equal to K.
body: A positive operator's singular values equal its nonnegative eigenvalues, counted with multiplicity and arranged in decreasing order. The previous min–max argument therefore gives each singular value of H no larger than the corresponding singular value of K. Consequently all Ky Fan sums of H are no larger than those of K. Every symmetric gauge, and hence every unitarily invariant norm, gives H no larger a value than K. Notice the two positive hypotheses in the statement.

slides.title: Apply the idea to rectangular maps
slides.lead: Let A and B have the same finite-dimensional input space, but perhaps different output spaces.
body: We cannot compare A and B directly in a Loewner order because they may not even be square or self-adjoint. We can, however, compare their source Gram operators, A adjoint A and B adjoint B. Those are both positive endomorphisms of the same input space. Suppose that for every input vector x, the squared length of A x is at most the squared length of B x. By the adjoint identity, these squared lengths are the quadratic forms of A adjoint A and B adjoint B. Therefore the Gram operator of A is below the Gram operator of B in Loewner order. Apply the min–max theorem to the two positive Gram operators.

slides.title: A rectangular numerical example
slides.lead: Take A from two-dimensional space to three-dimensional space with first output column of length three along the first coordinate axis, and second column of length one along the second output axis.
body: Take B to be a map with output lengths four and two on those same orthogonal input directions. Their source Gram matrices are diagonal: nine and one for A, sixteen and four for B. The difference is diagonal with entries seven and three, so it is positive. Therefore A adjoint A is below B adjoint B. The singular values of A are three and one. Those of B are four and two. The inequalities hold individually, and hence also for the operator, Frobenius, nuclear, and Ky Fan norms.

slides.title: Why squaring a form inequality can fail
slides.lead: There is another plausible but incorrect maneuver.
body: Suppose positive operators H and K satisfy H less than or equal to K. Can we square both sides and conclude H squared is below K squared? In general, no. Matrix multiplication is sensitive to noncommutativity, and the scalar observation that smaller nonnegative numbers have smaller squares does not automatically extend to noncommuting operators. We can make this failure completely explicit. Let H be the two-by-two diagonal matrix with entries one and zero. Let K have first row two, one, and second row one, one. First check positivity. H is positive.

slides.title: Trace inequalities versus singular-value inequalities
slides.lead: If H and K are positive and H is below K, their difference is positive.
body: The trace of a positive matrix is nonnegative, so trace H is at most trace K. This scalar trace inequality follows immediately from positivity and linearity. It is weaker than the complete eigenvalue comparison we obtained by min–max. For positive operators, the trace is the nuclear norm. Thus the trace comparison is one instance of an invariant-norm comparison. But trace control by itself does not imply operator-norm control. A matrix can have small total trace concentrated in one direction, while another has larger total trace spread across many directions.

slides.title: Prepare for the Sylvester equation
slides.lead: Soon we will meet an operator equation that asks us to recover an unknown map from a difference of two compositions.
body: A spectral-gap assumption will allow us to bound that unknown by the known defect. The estimates will involve norms, including Frobenius and general unitarily invariant norms. To manipulate them safely, we must recognize when a hypothesis controls a quadratic form, when it controls singular values, and when a separate argument is required for an operator-norm bound. Today's Gram and min–max argument is one standard bridge between these languages. It is powerful precisely because its hypotheses and conclusions are explicit.

slides.title: What to reconstruct
slides.lead: Prove the eigenvalue monotonicity statement directly from Courant–Fischer.
body: Then apply it to A adjoint A and B adjoint B to derive singular-value domination from inequalities of squared output lengths. Compute the singular values in the rectangular example. Verify every step in the two-by-two counterexample, including the positive difference K minus H and the negative determinant after squaring. Finally, explain why the negative-identity example defeats singular-value monotonicity for self-adjoint operators that are not positive.
